current.context: bep/imagemeta is a Go library for reading EXIF, IPTC and XMP image meta data from JPEG, TIFF, PNG, and WebP files. Prior to 0.17.3, imagemeta.Decode could exhaust memory when parsing PNG zTXt chunks whose keyword is "Raw profile type iptc": the declared chunk length can drive an allocation far larger than the input file, and the embedded zlib stream is decompressed without an output limit. The advisory reports a 42-byte input causing a 256 MB allocation and a 127 KB input inflating to 460 MB. The oversized-allocation path's memory effect depends on platform overcommit and configured GOMEMLIMIT or cgroup limits, while the decompression path reliably creates resident memory. Applications that decode untrusted PNGs with IPTC metadata processing can therefore suffer denial of service through memory exhaustion. This issue is fixed in 0.17.3.

current.context: Paymenter is a free and open-source webshop solution for management of hosting services. Prior to 1.5.7, the HasConfirmation trait in app/Livewire/Traits/HasConfirmation.php, included by app/Livewire/Component.php across 36 client-facing Livewire components, exposed executeConfirmedAction as a public action that invoked any component method accepted by method_exists. The action could call inherited InteractsWithProperties::fill(), whose data_set() writes arbitrary public properties, including state marked with #[Locked] and dotted paths into hydrated Eloquent models. Depending on the methods and properties exposed by an individual component, an unauthenticated caller could use this path to bypass intended authorization and modify server-side state intended to be immutable or protected from client-side manipulation. This issue is fixed in version 1.5.7.

current.context: TeamPass is a self-hosted collaborative password manager. Prior to 3.2.1.2, the update_folder action in app/sources/folders.queries.php allowed an authenticated, non-read-only user to re-parent a folder without checking whether the target folder or submitted parentId belonged to the caller's user-accessible_folders set. Selecting a personal folder as the new parent passed the personal-folder guard and set personal_folder on the target, transferring the credential subtree into the attacker's accessible space after the next login and hiding it from the organization, including administrators. The change exposed credential labels, logins, URLs, email addresses, and descriptions, while sharekey-protected passwords remained protected; hiding the subtree also denied other users access. This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.2.

current.context: Fabio is an HTTP(S) and TCP router for deploying applications managed by consul. Prior to 1.7.3, route/table.go selects targets using raw req.URL.Path, while proxy/http_proxy.go applies per-route ACL and basic-auth checks to the selected target and forwards the raw path to the origin. Dot-segment, encoded-dot, or repeated-slash variants can fall through to a less restrictive route that reaches the same backend; the backend then normalizes the path and serves the protected resource without the configured access controls. A less restrictive fallback route must reach the same backend; without one, the request returns 404. This issue is fixed in version 1.7.3.

current.context: pREST (PostgreSQL REST) is an API that delivers an application on top of a Postgres database. Prior to 2.4.0, the vulnerable parameter is _groupby, handled by GroupByClause in adapters/postgres/postgres.go. adapters/postgres/postgres.go uses the weaker isSafeSQLExpression check for this function-expression branch instead of the stricter single-field validator used for _select. That check validates only the outer function name against a 13-function allowlist and permits nested subqueries, trailing UNION syntax, and inner pg_ functions. controllers/crud.go concatenates the GROUP BY expression while parameterizing only WHERE values, allowing attacker-controlled SQL structure into the clause. Default configuration permits unauthenticated access; a restricted installation may require a low-privilege table reader. UNION-based extraction requires compatible column counts and types and was not verified end to end, but a delay-producing function can cause denial of service without that alignment. This issue is fixed in 2.4.0.

current.context: aMQTT is an open source MQTT broker and client. From 0.11.0 until 0.11.4, add_subscription() in amqtt/broker.py accepts malformed single-level + wildcard placement because it checks substrings instead of validating each slash-delimited level. The _matches() function converts each + into a greedy regular-expression fragment and evaluates it with re.fullmatch(), allowing a filter containing many adjacent + characters to trigger catastrophic backtracking when compared with a topic that partially matches but ultimately fails. Because matching runs synchronously in _run_broadcast(), one subscription followed by a publish can block the broker event loop, stopping message delivery and new connection processing until restart. Anonymous clients can trigger the issue with the default configuration. Any authenticated client permitted to create arbitrary subscriptions and publish messages may still exploit it when authentication is enabled. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.4.

current.context: OpenRemote is an open-source internet-of-things platform. Prior to 1.31.0, an authenticated user who obtains another user's MQTT session ID can disconnect that session across realm boundaries through the GET route GET {realm}/disconnect/{sessionID}. In manager/src/main/java/org/openremote/manager/security/UserResourceImpl.java, disconnectUserSession ignores the requested realm and calls mqttBrokerService.disconnectSession(sessionID) without checking session ownership; model/src/main/java/org/openremote/model/security/UserResource.java exposes the route without an @RolesAllowed restriction. The earlier cross-realm read-method guards did not cover this disconnect method, and same-realm users can also disconnect sessions they do not own. Session IDs are not trivially brute-forceable but may be exposed through monitoring, logs, or correlated API calls, and the unauthorized disconnect can disrupt MQTT connectivity across tenant boundaries without directly disclosing session data. This issue is fixed in 1.31.0.

current.context: Git LFS is a Git extension for versioning large files. From 0.6.0 until 3.8.1, Git LFS reads Git configuration options defined for a submodule without checking certain values for embedded line-ending control characters. A malicious repository can insert control characters such as line feed (LF) into those values to mimic options that cause Git LFS to execute an attacker-controlled command or binary while fetching or adding objects. This issue is fixed in version 3.8.1.

From 1.3.0 until 3.8.1, Git LFS does not correctly filter the limited set of options permitted in a repository's .lfsconfig file when option keys contain certain additional components. This issue is fixed in version 3.8.1.

current.context: Poweradmin is a web-based DNS administration tool for PowerDNS server. From 4.0.0 until 4.2.6, 4.3.5, and 4.4.1, lib/Domain/Service/MfaService.php verifies email second-factor codes through MfaService::verifyCode() without limiting failed attempts, and lib/Application/Controller/MfaVerifyController.php logs failures without throttling them. An attacker who knows the user's password can repeatedly guess the six-digit code during its ten-minute validity period when email MFA is enabled, potentially bypassing the second factor; the advisory notes MFA is disabled by default and that the practical request rate was not measured. This issue is fixed in versions 4.2.6, 4.3.5, and 4.4.1.

current.context: @fastify/static is the Fastify plugin for serving static files. In versions before 10.1.8, the allowedPath guard receives only the requested pathname, but the underlying send step selects the file to serve afterwards, so a request for a directory resolves to its default index file and an extensionless request resolves through the configured extensions to a matching file. The selected file is streamed without being re-checked against allowedPath, so a guard that denies a specific file is bypassed by requesting its directory or extensionless form. An unauthenticated client can read files inside the static root that the application meant to keep private whenever the denied file is reachable as a directory index or an extension match. The issue is fixed in @fastify/static 10.1.8, and users should upgrade to 10.1.8 or later. As a workaround, also deny the directory and extensionless forms in allowedPath, or disable the index and extensions options.

current.context: storyblok-backup is an npx CLI tool to create backups of a Storyblok space and restore individual resources. Prior to 0.7.1, the writeJson function used the editable Storyblok component name field as a filename without path containment. A person with component-management access in a Storyblok space could store a component name containing path traversal sequences; when another user later ran a backup for that space, the stored name escaped the configured backup directory and caused a JSON file to be written outside it on the backup host. Depending on the path chosen and the backup process's permissions, this could overwrite existing files at attacker-chosen locations. The vulnerability is specific to components: stories and datasources use numeric identifiers, and asset names are reduced to a final path segment. This issue is fixed in version 0.7.1.

current.context: Go-Guerrilla SMTP Daemon is a lightweight SMTP server written in Go. In 1.6.7 and earlier, according to the repository advisory's structured affected range, server.go defines the seven-byte cmdXCLIENT token, but the XCLIENT handler slices input[8:] after matching only that seven-byte verb, so a bare command causes an out-of-bounds panic in handleClient and terminates the daemon because that connection goroutine does not recover the panic. The issue is reachable by an unauthenticated client when the non-default xclient_on setting is enabled; no HELO command is required. The repository fix is present in version 1.6.7-1.

current.context: The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection.

The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched.  The names already rewritten are freed, but their pointers stay in the result vector, and the error path frees them again with globfree.

The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

current.context: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions before 11.6.10, it rejects destinations containing parent-directory path segments by an exact string match, so a segment that carries a semicolon path parameter, such as a dot-dot segment followed by a semicolon and an optional parameter, is not equal to the plain dot-dot form and passes the check, and the WHATWG URL parser keeps it as an ordinary segment so the rewrite-prefix containment check also passes. Servlet containers such as Apache Tomcat and Jetty strip semicolon path parameters from each segment before resolving dot-segments, so a request routed through the configured prefix is rewritten and reaches the upstream where it resolves above the intended subtree, escaping the path the proxy is meant to expose and, on some containers, crossing application contexts. Both the HTTP and WebSocket proxy paths are affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

current.context: @fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions before 12.8.4, its buildURL function rejects parent-directory path segments by an exact string match, so a segment that carries a semicolon path parameter, such as a dot-dot segment followed by a semicolon and an optional parameter, is not equal to the plain dot-dot form and passes the traversal check, and the WHATWG URL parser keeps it as an ordinary segment so the base-prefix containment check also passes. Backends that strip semicolon path parameters before resolving dot-segments, such as Apache Tomcat, Jetty, WildFly, and Spring Boot, turn the segment back into a parent-directory reference and resolve it, so an unauthenticated client can escape the intended upstream prefix and reach internal paths such as admin or internal API endpoints, including with state-changing methods. Deployments that proxy to Node.js, nginx, or Express upstreams are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.4, and users should upgrade to 12.8.4 or later.

current.context: NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.9.4 to 3.10.3, NLTK ZIP package extraction can write through an existing in-root hardlink whose other link points outside the NLTK data root. A local attacker who can prepare the extraction target can cause a package member write to overwrite an out-of-root file, violating the pathsec containment boundary and affecting integrity and availability. This issues is fixed in version 3.10.4.

current.context: NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.9.4 until 3.10.4, NLTK corpus-reader path pointers and view methods validate a requested relative path without consistently resolving intermediate directory symlinks against the reader's scoped root. A local attacker who can place such a symlink can make abspaths or words reach a readable file outside the corpus root and disclose its contents. On releases with pathsec enforcement, the file must remain inside a global NLTK allowed root; version 3.9.4 has enforcement disabled and permits a broader escape. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

current.context: NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.6 to 3.10.3, XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment accumulates 1 KiB blocks and repeatedly applies whole-buffer XML validation while a comment or CDATA terminator remains ahead. A large comment in an attacker-controlled corpus file causes quadratic CPU consumption through documented XML corpus readers across the affected range. On 3.6 and 3.9.2, a large CDATA section incurs the quadratic scan before rejection, while on 3.10.3 both comment and CDATA documents are read successfully. This vulnerability is fixed in 3.10.4.

current.context: NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.6.7 until 3.10.4, nltk.downloader follows collection membership without tracking already visited collection nodes. A self-referencing or mutually referencing collection index can therefore make the package-closure walk loop indefinitely while its queue and memory usage grow, denying service when a victim processes the attacker-influenced index. Prior to 3.10.4, WordNet Synset.tree and acyclic_tree traverse relation graphs through recursive utility helpers without a depth bound. cisa_kev.title: Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability
cisa_kev.description: Apache Roller contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. This CVE covers the same underlying vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384 but applies to a broader range of affected versions.
cisa_kev.required_action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.

nvd.description:
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.

This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited.

Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Users who cannot upgrade right away should set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restart Roller. Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.

current.context: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.0.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, it takes every upgraded socket and dispatches the request through the Fastify router before the WebSocket library takes ownership of the socket. Node.js removes its own error listener from the socket before emitting the upgrade event, and the plugin does not attach one of its own during routing, so a socket error such as a client connection reset that arrives before the WebSocket library takes over is unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. The error window is open whenever anything asynchronous runs between dispatch and the route handler, such as an async hook on the proxied route or any unrelated async route in the application. A single unauthenticated upgrade request followed by a connection reset is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

current.context: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.4.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, a WebSocket upgrade request whose path carries a URL fragment is matched by the router and answered with a successful upgrade before the upstream link is created. Building the upstream target then throws, the error is only logged, and the accepted client socket is left open with no error listener, so the next frame the client sends becomes an unhandled error and terminates the Node.js process. A request target that is not a valid URL reference reaching a parameterized prefix triggers the same path. A single unauthenticated upgrade request followed by one frame is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

current.context: The MongoDB Rust Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

current.context: A MongoDB C# Driver component that interprets connection configuration supplied by the hosting application can include the caller-supplied configuration value in the text of the error it raises when that value cannot be interpreted. The redaction applied to that text does not cover all forms in which secret material may appear, so authentication material embedded in the configuration value can be preserved in the resulting error text and in anything that records it. Exploitation requires only the low privilege needed to observe the application's own error output or logs on the system where the driver runs; no database credentials or server connectivity are required. The result is disclosure of sensitive information to parties whose access to error output is broader than their intended access to the configuration secret.

current.context: Tamari is a fully-featured recipe manager web application built using Python and the Flask Framework. Prior to 1.7.2, an authenticated user can bypass the recipe-autofill SSRF check by submitting a hostname under the user's control through the Autofill from URL feature; the hostname can resolve to a public address during validation and a private or internal address during the later connection. In app/myrecipes/routes.py, is_safe_autofill_url validates the first DNS response, but recipe autofill passes the original URL to requests.get, which independently resolves the hostname and can connect to the internal address. The fetched response is parsed into recipe fields, enabling internal-service reconnaissance and potential data exposure; no redirect is required, and disabling redirects does not stop this DNS-rebinding bypass. This issue is fixed in 1.7.2.

current.context: aMQTT is an open source MQTT broker and client. From 0.11.0 until 0.12.1, the QoS 2 transaction handler in amqtt/mqtt/protocol/handler.py, _handle_qos2_message_flow(), can retain transaction state and packet identifiers when a client disconnects before the handshake completes, unlike QoS 1 flows that expire after the default five-second timeout. A remote client can repeatedly begin QoS 2 flows and disconnect without maintaining long-lived connections; anonymous clients can do this with the default configuration, while authenticated deployments remain affected when a client may initiate QoS 2 flows. The retained state grows broker memory until resource exhaustion can terminate the process; no confidentiality or integrity impact is identified. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.1.

current.context: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.0.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, a WebSocket upgrade that is pipelined behind another HTTP request on the same cleartext connection arrives while that request's response is still attached to the socket. The shared upgrade listener sees the socket is already claimed and returns early without taking the upgrade, but it does not attach an error listener to the raw socket, and Node.js has already removed its own error listener before emitting the upgrade event. A later socket error on that connection, such as a client connection reset, is therefore unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. A single unauthenticated connection that pipelines an upgrade behind a normal request and then resets is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. Upgrades over TLS are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

current.context: @fastify/static is the Fastify plugin for serving static files. In versions up to and including 10.1.11, when it is configured to deny or ignore dotfiles together with directory listing enabled, a request for a denied dot-directory returns its directory listing instead of being refused. The underlying send step answers with a forbidden response, but the listing fallback misreads that response on a path ending in a slash as a directory without an index file and serves the listing anyway. An unauthenticated client can enumerate the names of files and subdirectories, recursively, inside dot-directories the operator explicitly denied, such as version control, backup, and key file names. File contents remain protected and only names are disclosed. The issue is fixed in @fastify/static 10.1.12, and users should upgrade to 10.1.12 or later. As a workaround, disable directory listing or do not serve a root that contains dot-directories.

current.context: @fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions 12.8.1 through 12.8.3, its buildURL function checked the attacker-supplied source string for parent-directory segments, but when the source begins with the same special scheme as the base, such as http or https, the WHATWG URL parser drops the scheme and resolves the remainder as a relative path. A payload that glues the scheme to a percent-encoded parent-directory sequence therefore passes the check, because the inspected segment reads as the scheme plus the dots rather than a bare parent-directory token, while the proxy forwards the encoded traversal unchanged. An upstream that percent-decodes the request path before resolving dot-segments then serves a path outside the configured prefix, so an unauthenticated client scoped to an upstream prefix, or relying on Fastify route guards in front of the proxy, can escape that prefix and reach sibling or parent upstream endpoints. The per-segment check added in 12.8.1 is what the scheme prefix bypasses, and releases up to 12.8.0 already rejected the decoded form. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.4, and users should upgrade to 12.8.4 or later.

The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not preserve quoted search argument boundaries when it processes a dashboard search.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role, should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could inject arbitrary fields into Splunk Enterprise audit records via the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. 
Successful exploitation could allow the unauthenticated user to forge audit evidence, compromising the integrity of audit reviews and security detections that rely on legacy audit-field parsing.

current.context:
In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission and restricted tenant access could modify settings for a tenant outside the role scope through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. With this access, the user could expose confidential tenant environment values, alter tenant settings and automation behavior, or take the tenant out of operation.
The vulnerability is possible because the Tenant REST API checks the System Settings edit permission but does not enforce the tenant restrictions for the role before it updates the selected tenant.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises), Configure multiple tenants on your Splunk SOAR (On-premises) instance (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.7.0/configure-product-settings-for-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance/configure-multiple-tenants-on-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance), and REST Tenant (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/8.5.0/multi-tenancy-endpoints/rest-tenant) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to edit containers for an allowed label could forge the author attribution of container pins and access limited user details outside the expected authorization boundary.
The Container Pin Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not prevent caller-provided author fields from reaching generic model binding, which lets the request reassign a pin author or query user-related data outside the expected authorization scope.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Assets edit or delete permission and access to one or more tenants could change or delete assets assigned to other tenants through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. current.context:
United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP GetConfiguration Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP messages. When parsing GetConfiguration requests, the process does not properly validate the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28968.

current.context: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 7.1.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, it opens the upstream WebSocket connection with a header set built by the default header rewriter, which forwards the client cookie but never sets the upstream origin option, so the browser origin header is dropped while the authenticating cookie is forwarded. Many WebSocket servers defend against cross-site hijacking by checking the origin and treat a missing origin as a trusted non-browser client, so behind the proxy that check never sees the foreign origin. A malicious page visited by a logged-in user can therefore open a WebSocket through the proxy to an upstream that authenticates the handshake with a cookie, and read or send messages on the user's behalf. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later. As a workaround, provide a header rewriter that sets a correct origin, or validate the origin before the proxy.

current.context: When extra data is allowed (extra=Extra.allow), providing a __pydantic_initialised__ key when validating a Pydantic V1 dataclass makes it considered as already validated, resulting in field values not being validated. The __init__() method of Pydantic V1 dataclasses stores all the provided keyword arguments in the instance __dict__ before validation, so a __pydantic_initialised__ keyword argument overrides the internal flag used to skip validation of already validated instances. As a result, data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into Pydantic V1 dataclasses allowing extra data. The issue was fixed in Pydantic 1.10.27. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

current.context:
The preview mode of the OPC (OnPage Composer) page
builder of JTL-Shop is activated by a request parameter alone and
renders page data supplied in the request without checking for an authenticated
backend session with the corresponding permission. Several portlet properties
are output without output encoding. An unauthenticated remote attacker
can thereby cause script code to be executed in the browser of a
visitor or administrator who opens a crafted link; in the case of an
administrator, actions can be performed with the administrator's privileges. Third-party
plugins whose portlets evaluate property values as templates can
additionally be made to execute template code through the same entry point. This is
a separate flaw in such plugins and does not affect the portlets of JTL-Shop itself.

current.context: django-docutils provides reStructuredText support for Django. Prior to 0.30.0, public rendering paths including publish_doctree, publish_html_from_source, publish_html_from_doctree, publish_parts_from_doctree, the {% rst %} template tag, the rst template filter, DocutilsTemplates, and DocutilsView pass lower-trust reStructuredText to Docutils without disabling file_insertion_enabled, raw_enabled, ambient docutils.conf processing, or unsafe URI schemes and without consistently sanitizing doctrees. An attacker who can influence rendered reStructuredText can use include or csv-table directives to read local files or cause server-side URL requests, or use raw HTML and unsafe URI output to inject stored script-capable content. Applications that render only trusted static reStructuredText are not affected unless attackers can influence it. This issue is fixed in version 0.30.0.

current.context: HTSlib is a library for reading and writing bioinformatics file formats. Prior to 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24, cram_index_load does not verify that the number of reference sequences in a CRAM .crai index does not exceed the CRAM header reference count. A malformed index can drive unbounded index-array allocation, and when the number of references in the index is within two of INT_MAX, the growth calculation can wrap, read beyond a heap buffer, and use the resulting value as a pointer for an unchecked memory write. Any region query can trigger the flaw, causing denial of service or memory corruption. This issue is fixed in versions 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24.

current.context: HTSlib is a library for reading and writing bioinformatics file formats. Prior to 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24, fai_retrieve does not verify that the line width recorded in a FASTA .fai index is greater than or equal to the number of bases per line. When the line width is exactly one less than the base count, retrieval allocates an undersized heap buffer and writes one byte beyond its end; larger discrepancies instead cause an allocation failure that is handled. This issue can corrupt heap memory and crash the process. This issue is fixed in versions 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24.

current.context: HTSlib is a library for reading and writing bioinformatics file formats. Prior to 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24, the experimental CRAM v4 XPACK and XRLE decoders cache expanded block pointers at indexes beyond the 512-element slice->block_by_id array. An array index partially controlled by data in the input file first causes an out-of-bounds read to determine whether a block is cached; a null value then causes allocation of a block and an out-of-bounds pointer write to the same element. The invalid read may crash the process, while the write may corrupt heap state and could permit arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in versions 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24.

current.context: HTSlib is a library for reading and writing bioinformatics file formats. Prior to 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24, the CRAM decoder validates the 254-character query-name limit only after decoding the name into a 1024-byte stack array. An attacker-controlled CRAM record can provide an overlong query name and overflow the local stack buffer before the later validation runs; all CRAM format versions are affected. Opening such a file can crash the process, corrupt stack data, and may permit arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in versions 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24.

current.context: Git LFS is a Git extension for versioning large files. From 0.5.0 until 3.8.1, Git LFS does not format the SSH URL path component as a single argument when constructing remote object-transfer or authentication commands. Shell metacharacters in the SSH URL can therefore escape the intended path argument and cause arbitrary command execution when the remote Git LFS service passes received commands to a shell without adequate sanitization. Git LFS also incorrectly encodes default HTTPS URLs when an SSH URL is configured and the remote host either does not support Git LFS remote commands over SSH or supports HTTP authentication over SSH but git-lfs-authenticate does not return an explicit HTTP URL. This issue is fixed in version 3.8.1.

Authorization headers are never forwarded to inappropriate hosts and are not the affected secret in this vulnerability. This issue is fixed in version 3.8.1.

current.context: Cisco Expressway Series contains a use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service.

cisa_kev.title: Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability
cisa_kev.description: Cisco Expressway Series contains a use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service.
cisa_kev.required_action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.

nvd.description:
A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.

This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies. Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated. An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.
Note: Cisco Expressway Series refers to Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) devices and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) devices.

current.context: Jupyter MCP Server is a Model Context Protocol server for Jupyter. Prior to 1.0.3, standalone streamable-http mode can enforce MCP_TOKEN on /mcp while leaving the state-changing /api/connect and /api/stop management routes unauthenticated. An unauthenticated network caller can use /api/connect to replace runtime_url and document_url values and their tokens, reset ServerContext, and start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure, causing the server to send Jupyter API and WebSocket traffic to that backend. The caller can also use /api/stop to stop the current notebook kernel. This boundary failure does not require explicit insecure no-auth mode and occurs outside normal MCP JSON-RPC tool dispatch. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.3.

An unauthenticated network caller can use /api/connect to replace runtime_url and document_url values and their tokens, reset ServerContext, and start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure, causing the server to send Jupyter API and WebSocket traffic to that backend. The caller can also use /api/stop to stop the current notebook kernel. This boundary failure does not require explicit insecure no-auth mode and occurs outside normal MCP JSON-RPC tool dispatch. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.3.

current.context: Aperi'Solve is an open-source steganalysis web platform. Prior to 3.4.2, an unauthenticated user can submit a PNG to POST /upload, which reaches aperisolve/utils/png.py through analyze_image, PCRTAnalyzer, PNG.repair(), and check_idat(). A malformed IDAT chunk can make attacker-controlled length and newline data drive an unbounded combinations search in PNG._fix_dos2unix(), causing repeated CRC checks that occupy a worker and delay or block image analysis for other users. Per-IP upload limits and eventual job termination bound the denial of service, and the issue has no confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 3.4.2.

current.context: Sprout Track is a self-hosted baby tracking application. Prior to 1.3.5, Sprout Track uses a publicly known hardcoded signing secret when JWT_SECRET is unset, and standard setup does not generate a unique secret. On a network-reachable affected deployment, an unauthenticated attacker can sign JWTs with arbitrary claims, including system-administrator claims, to access administrative functionality and read or modify family, child activity, account, and email data. Deployments with a strong unique JWT_SECRET are not affected. Managed and hosted instances were reported remediated. This issue is fixed in version 1.3.5.

current.context: Jupyter MCP Server is a Model Context Protocol server for Jupyter. Prior to 1.0.3, standalone streamable-http mode validates Host and Origin values for /mcp but does not apply the same browser-origin controls to the state-changing /api/connect and /api/stop management routes. The default broad bind can increase exposure, but the vulnerability is the missing management-route origin boundary, not a lack of Host validation on /mcp. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.3.

current.context: Daptin is a GraphQL/JSON-API headless CMS. Prior to 0.12.30, the generic GET /api/{entity} list endpoint accepts attacker-controlled sort values in PaginatedFindAllWithoutFilters in server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go without validating the requested column against the table schema. The code uses those values for SELECT and ORDER BY identifier construction, so an embedded identifier quote can terminate the quoted identifier and make the remainder parse as SQL, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to extract unauthorized table data through blind or error-based behavior or repeatedly trigger query failures. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.30.

current.context: Daptin is a GraphQL/JSON-API headless CMS. From 0.11.4 until 0.12.30, the generic GET /yjs/:documentName WebSocket route in InitializeYjsResources requires a session but does not authorize the database resource selected by a typename.referenceId.columnName room name. current.context: falcon-rust is a Rust implementation of the Falcon post-quantum signature scheme. Prior to 0.2.0, the discrete-Gaussian sampler in src/samplerz.rs evaluates approx_exp, ber_exp, and sampler_z acceptance probabilities with FixedPoint64 values having only 32 fractional bits. The scaling in approx_exp quantizes its input and limits relative precision to about 2^-33, below Falcon's required bound, causing reference known-answer vectors to diverge and invalidating the proof assumption that secret-dependent signature and key distributions are negligibly close to the ideal discrete Gaussian. This is a cryptographic-soundness defect and no practical key-recovery attack has been demonstrated. This issue is fixed in version 0.2.0.

current.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: always encode the origin fh when index is enabled

On an overlay with index=on,nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory
crashes the kernel once an LSM has started to deny CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH
to the mounter, the task that mounted the overlay. The mount and the LSM
policy change require root. After that, any user who can write to a
directory that exists only in a lower layer triggers the oops by doing
so.

Before a file or directory that exists only in a lower layer is changed
for the first time, overlayfs copies it to the writable upper layer.
This is called copy up.

On copy up, ovl_get_origin_fh() encodes the file handle of the lower
inode, called the origin. It returns NULL if ovl_can_decode_fh() says
that the lower filesystem cannot decode handles. Whether the callers can
handle NULL depends on the index option:

- Without an index, NULL is fine: the callers store an empty origin
  xattr.
- With index enabled, overlayfs keeps entries for copied up inodes in an
  internal index directory. The name of an index entry is derived from
  the handle, so ovl_get_origin_fh() must return a handle or an error.

The mount only enables the index if ovl_can_decode_fh() succeeds for all
layers, but the result can change later. The function checks the export
operations of the filesystem and capable(CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH). Copy up
runs with the mounter's credentials, and an LSM can start to deny the
capability to those credentials after the mount. ovl_get_origin_fh()
then returns NULL with index enabled.

This goes wrong in two callers:

- With nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory creates an index entry for
  the directory. ovl_create_index() passes the NULL handle to
  ovl_get_index_name_fh(), which dereferences it.
- If the result changes while mount(2) is still running,
  ovl_get_indexdir() passes a NULL from ovl_get_origin_fh() to
  ovl_verify_set_fh() in the same way.

Before the commit in the Fixes tag, these two callers encoded the handle
themselves, without consulting ovl_can_decode_fh().

Reproduced with a BPF LSM program that started to deny the capability
after the mount. An unprivileged touch in a directory that had not been
copied up yet oopsed in ovl_get_index_name_fh(). With this patch the
touch succeeds and the directory gets its index entry.

Fix this by calling ovl_can_decode_fh() in ovl_get_origin_fh() only when
index is disabled.

current.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: use the pinned upper dir in ovl_fix_origin()

Renames made directly on the upper filesystem during a lookup crash the
kernel.

A dentry that is passed to vfs_setxattr() must be pinned.
ovl_fix_origin() passes upper->d_parent to ovl_set_impure() without a
reference, and the lookup holds no lock of the upper directory. A
rename on the upper filesystem changes d_parent, and only the child
pins the new parent, so a second rename and an rmdir free it.

With delays in ovl_fix_origin() and ovl_set_impure(), renaming the upper
directory twice and removing the intermediate parent during the lookup
of a merge directory without an origin xattr gave a KASAN
use-after-free in vfs_setxattr().

Fix this by passing the upper dentry that the overlay parent holds.

[amir: add helper ovl_set_impure_dir()]

current.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: take a snapshot of the name for copy up

The copy up of a directory reads a freed dentry name when a lookup
moves the directory at the same time.

A pointer to the name of a dentry is only valid while something stops
a move of the dentry. ovl_do_copy_up() keeps a plain copy of
c->dentry->d_name in c->destname, and ovl_copy_up_start() only keeps
ovl_rename() away. When a lookup finds the same directory under another
name after a change to the lower layer, d_splice_alias() moves the
dentry and frees its external name.

With a delay in ovl_do_copy_up(), a chmod of a lower-only directory with
a 60 byte name raced with a rename of that directory in the lower layer
and a stat of the new name, and KASAN reported a use-after-free in
lookup_noperm_common().

Fix this by using take_dentry_name_snapshot() for c->destname.

current.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: set OVL_WHITEOUTS before publishing the upper dir

Listing a directory while it is copied up causes a use-after-free of
the readdir cache.

A merge directory must never be iterated as a real upper directory:
that mode frees the cache in OVL_I(inode)->cache without looking at
its refcount, while files opened in merged mode still use it.
ovl_copy_up_workdir() publishes the upper dentry before it sets
OVL_WHITEOUTS, and ovl_dir_open() samples both without a lock, so an
open between the two stores finds the upper directory and takes it
for a real one.

With a delay between the two stores, an unprivileged process that
listed a directory during its copy-up saw only "." and "..", and its
next getdents freed the readdir cache of another descriptor.

Fix this by setting OVL_WHITEOUTS before ovl_inode_update(), so that
ovl_dir_reset() agrees with ovl_dir_open(), and by testing
OVL_TYPE_MERGE() of the path type in ovl_dir_open(), so that an open
that observes the upper dentry never iterates a merge dir as a real
dir, regardless of the order in which it observes the flag.

[amir: test OVL_TYPE_MERGE() instead of smp_rmb() in ovl_dir_open()]

current.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir

Listing a directory on an overlay uses a freed dentry and crashes the
kernel when a lookup moves the directory at the same time.

Code that can sleep may only use d_parent without a reference while
something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_iterate_real(),
ovl_need_adjust_d_ino() and ovl_cache_update() use the d_parent of the
listed directory and hold only the lock of that directory. When a

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir

Listing a directory on an overlay uses a freed dentry and crashes the
kernel when a lookup moves the directory at the same time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: hold server info until cifsd exits

The last session reference can be dropped while the cifsd demultiplex
thread is still running clean_demultiplex_info(). That thread frees
TCP_Server_Info there, racing with cifs_put_tcp_session() as it releases
the server crypto state. syzbot reported a KASAN use-after-free in
cifs_crypto_secmech_release().

Keep an object reference for the cifsd thread. Defer final crypto,
session-key, network namespace, string, and structure cleanup until both
the last session reference and the thread reference are dropped. Drop the
thread reference after clean_demultiplex_info() has finished using the
server.

Build-tested with ARCH=arm64 and W=1 for
fs/smb/client/connect.o. The KASAN reproducer was not run on the patched
kernel.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix OOB last_entry pointer from unbounded LastNameOffset

CIFSFindFirst() and CIFSFindNext() locate the last entry of a
TRANS2_FIND_FIRST2 or TRANS2_FIND_NEXT2 response by adding the
LastNameOffset of the response parameters to the start of the data
area, and store the result in psrch_inf->last_entry. MS-CIFS 2.2.6.2.2
defines that offset as the offset of the entry's file name; the client
follows the reading of NT and Samba servers, which point it at the
entry. LastNameOffset is only checked against CIFSMaxBufSize, which
says nothing about the response actually received: validate_t2() lets
the data area start up to 1024 bytes into the buffer, and SendReceive()
copies at most CIFSMaxBufSize + MAX_CIFS_HDR_SIZE bytes of a response,
16468 by default, into a cifs_request allocation of CIFSMaxBufSize +
MAX_SMB2_HDR_SIZE bytes, 16588 by default. The pointer itself can
therefore be placed anywhere from the end of the received data to 820
bytes past the end of the allocation.

The read through that pointer is far larger than its displacement.
find_cifs_entry() hands last_entry to cifs_save_resume_key() after every
FindNext and after the FindFirst of a search rewind, and
cifs_fill_dirent() takes the length of the name from the entry itself: a
__le32 FileNameLength for most levels, a __u8 for
SMB_FIND_FILE_INFO_STANDARD, and for SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the result of a
scan for the terminating NUL over up to PATH_MAX + 1 UTF-16 units. The
name is recorded as the resume name of the search, and the next
CIFSFindNext() rejects only a recorded length of PATH_MAX or more before
copying the name into the ResumeFileName of its request and sending it
with the resume key taken from the same entry: up to 4 KiB of memory
from past the end of the allocation leaks to the server, and for
SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the NUL scan runs about twice as far before the
length is even known. The entry does not have to lie outside the
response for that either: a maximal response ends about 120 bytes before
the end of the allocation, so an entry in its last bytes with a name
just under PATH_MAX has nearly all of that name copied from past the
allocation.

It needs nothing unusual from the client: a FindNext response that
reports no entries and does not end the search makes find_cifs_entry()
send the next FindNext at once, carrying whatever was parsed at
LastNameOffset, and a search rewind can do the same after its
FindFirst. SMB1 is not negotiated by default: this takes a malicious
or compromised server, a mount of it with an explicit vers=1.0, which
CONFIG_CIFS_ALLOW_INSECURE_LEGACY (default y) permits, and a directory
listing on that mount.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: snapshot dentry names in file and setattr traces

Patch series "ocfs2: stabilize dentry names in file and setattr traces",
v4.

Snapshot names at all six users of ocfs2__file_ops and at the separate
setattr event. Patch 1 handles the five ordinary file-operation callers
and setattr. Patch 2 handles release separately to preserve its locked
open-count sample and take the snapshot outside that critical section.

The release explanation distinguishes its existing RCU lifetime coverage
from name/length consistency. It does not claim that the ordinary
callers' external-name UAF interleaving crosses the held inode spinlock.
The release source change is unchanged from v3.

Patch 1 also removes the read callback's redundant NULL-inode check.
The two patches apply independently and leave trace formats unchanged.


This patch (of 2):

The open, fsync, read, write and splice-read trace calls pass the live
dentry name and length to the shared ocfs2__file_ops event class.
ocfs2_setattr() passes the same unprotected arguments to its own event.
Both events size and copy a __string field separately. A reference to
the dentry does not pin the external storage backing an individual name.

With an event enabled, a caller can be preempted after loading the name
pointer. A long-to-short rename can then replace the name and reclaim its
old external allocation before the trace callback sizes or copies it,
provided no other snapshot retains that allocation.

The setattr inode lock does not exclude every rename: a same-directory
rename of a source directory need not take that directory's inode lock.
It can therefore change the dentry name while setattr records its event.
Inline names and separately loaded lengths can also change during trace
record sizing and copying.

Take a dentry name snapshot around each of these six trace calls and
pass both the string and length from the snapshot. Check event enablement
before taking a snapshot. Keep the event classes and formats unchanged.

Also remove the redundant NULL-inode check in the read callback.
file_inode() returns the open file's inode, which is already used by the
trace call above the check.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: pin refcount trees before dropping the lookup lock

A refcount tree returned to ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() must stay alive
until that caller releases its operation reference. However,
ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() returns the cached pointer after dropping
osb_lock, and the caller only takes its kref afterwards. The registry
reference does not protect this gap from concurrent removal.

This can happen when another node frees a refcount root and reuses its
block with a different generation while this mount retains the old
cached tree. Two local operations on different inodes sharing the new
root, such as data CoW and an external xattr update, can then look up
the same stale tree. Their inode locks are independent, and both the
REFCOUNT DLM lock and rf_sem are acquired after the first operation
reference.

The following ordering is possible, with no other operation references:

  Data CoW                         Xattr update
  --------                         ------------
  Look up the old tree under
    osb_lock, then drop osb_lock
                                   Look up the same tree and take a kref
                                   Acquire the tree locks and read the
                                     new on-disk generation
                                   Erase the old tree under osb_lock
                                   Unlock and drop the operation kref
                                   Drop the registry kref, freeing tree
  Take a kref through the
    freed tree pointer

The final kref_get() accesses freed rf_getcnt storage, and subsequent
accesses in ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() also use the freed allocation.

Take the operation reference in ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() before
releasing osb_lock, including when an insertion loses to another lookup.
Removal must acquire the same lock, so it cannot drop the registry
reference before the lookup has pinned the tree. Keep the existing
unlock and error path puts. The two callers that already hold the
refcount tree lock keep their borrowed lookup behavior and do not
acquire an extra reference.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: fix chunk number of the first chunk in a local quota file

Mounting a crafted OCFS2 image can corrupt kernel memory.  When the
local quota file header of such an image claims zero chunks, the first
quota entry allocated during the mount gets a chunk number taken from a
kernel pointer, and releasing that entry clears a bit far outside the
chunk bitmap.

The write will corrupt the data stored at that address, and the
corruption may lead to a system crash or damage unrelated data. 
Mounting requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so it takes an untrusted image, such
as removable media or a loop mount of a file from elsewhere.

Since the chunk number comes from a kernel pointer, the address of the
bit that gets cleared differs from boot to boot, and the issue has been
reported under several titles:

- BUG: unable to handle kernel paging request in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: slab-use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KFENCE: use-after-free write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot

Note that none of these is a use-after-free in the quota code: the
chunk and its buffer head are alive.  The bit that gets cleared lies
far outside the bitmap.  KASAN and KFENCE name each report based on the
object occupying that address, which explains why the same issue is
reported under so many different titles.  In the report I sent, the
address fell in a free page, which KASAN labels use-after-free.

There are known reproducers.  Both a syzkaller and a C reproducer are
available from the Google Drive link [1] in my report thread.  The
issue was found by our modified syzkaller, not a theoretical thing
found by an LLM.  I have not seen it outside fuzzing, so it is not
affecting me in the real world.

The local quota file in OCFS2 is divided into chunks, and each chunk
begins with a header block holding a bitmap of the quota entries that
chunk has handed out.  Chunks are numbered from zero, and that number is
used to convert the file offset of an entry back into a bit position in
the bitmap.  ocfs2_local_quota_add_chunk() appends a new chunk to the
in-memory list and numbers it one past the chunk that was last:

	list_add_tail(&chunk->qc_chunk, &oinfo->dqi_chunk);
	chunk->qc_num = list_entry(chunk->qc_chunk.prev,
				   struct ocfs2_quota_chunk,
				   qc_chunk)->qc_num + 1;

The predecessor is looked up after the new chunk is added to the list, so
if the list was empty, the prev pointer is the list head itself.  The head
is the dqi_chunk member of struct ocfs2_mem_dqinfo and is not a chunk, so
reading qc_num through it lands 16 bytes past the start of the head, on
the dqi_gqinode pointer that follows it.  The first chunk of the file is
then numbered with the lower half of a kernel pointer instead of 0.

The list is empty when the local quota file header claims the file has no
chunks.  ocfs2_local_read_info() takes dqi_chunks from that header without
validating it, so an image with dqi_chunks == 0 takes this path when the
first quota entry is allocated.

ocfs2_create_local_dquot() turns the bad number into a file offset with
ol_dqblk_off(), which shifts a 32-bit block number left by the block size
bits, so the top bits of such a large block number are lost. 
ocfs2_local_release_dquot() turns the offset back into a bit index with
ol_dqblk_chunk_off(), using the full chunk number, so the lost bits push
that index far outside the bitmap, and clearing it corrupts unrelated
memory.

Compute the chunk number before putting the chunk on the list, and use 0
when the list is empty.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: cancel quota sync work before freeing quota info

OCFS2 quota info owns dqi_sync_work and must outlive both its timer and
qsync_work_fn().  ocfs2_local_free_info() frees that owner without
cancelling the work, relying on the quota suspend/disable wrappers.

Loading quotas on a read-only to read-write remount can successfully queue
the work in ocfs2_global_read_info() and then fail while attaching a dquot
to an existing inode in add_dquot_ref().  The quota core unwinds that
failure directly through dquot_disable(), bypassing the OCFS2 wrapper:

  Remount task (s_umount write)        Timer/workqueue
  ocfs2_global_read_info()
    schedules dqi_sync_work
  add_dquot_ref() returns an error
  dquot_disable()
    ocfs2_local_free_info()
      frees oinfo
                                     delayed-work timer expires
                                     qsync_work_fn() reads oinfo

The timer core can then write to the freed embedded timer, or
qsync_work_fn() can read oinfo->dqi_gqinode before its s_umount trylock.
The outer ocfs2_disable_quotas() cleanup skips the failed type because
dquot_disable() has already cleared its loaded state.

Cancel dqi_sync_work synchronously at the start of
ocfs2_local_free_info(), before dropping the global inode or freeing any
owner state. The work is initialized whenever read_file_info() succeeds.
dquot_disable() holds s_umount for write, so the callback skips its quota
scan via down_read_trylock() and can finish without waiting for teardown.
The synchronous cancel also handles its self-rearm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: hold the lookup reference across convert AST enqueue

dlm_convert_lock_handler() drops the reference it took when it found the
lock on res->granted at its leave label, one statement before it calls
dlm_queue_ast().  dlm_free_dead_locks() takes res->spinlock and drops the
list and base references, so a peer death landing in that gap leaves the
handler's own put as the one that frees the lock, and __dlm_queue_ast()
then reads lock->lockres from freed memory.

The handler is registered next to dlm_create_lock_handler(), so a convert
message buffered on a dying peer's socket arrives on the same o2net
receive work that o2net_disconnect_node() does not wait for.  The two can
interleave as follows, with the reference counts as they are before this
fix:

  Socket data-ready       Node-down thread      Receive worker
  -----------------       ----------------      --------------
  o2net_data_ready()
    select sc under
    callback read lock
                          o2net_disconnect_node()
                            queue shutdown
                            begin flush; new color
    queue sc_rx_work
    in the new color
    release callback lock
                            shutdown socket
                            flush returns
                                                read buffered convert_lock
                                                dlm_convert_lock_handler()
                                                  find lock on res->granted
                                                  dlm_lock_get()  refs = 3
                                                  lock res->spinlock
                                                  __dlmconvert_master()
                                                    call_ast = 1
                                                  unlock res->spinlock
                          DLM node-down cleanup
                            lock res->spinlock
                            dlm_free_dead_locks()
                              unlink lock
                              put list ref  refs = 2
                              put base ref  refs = 1
                            unlock res->spinlock
                                                dlm_lock_put()  refs = 0
                                                  free lock
                                                dlm_queue_ast()
                                                  __dlm_queue_ast()
                                                  read lock->lockres
                                                  (use-after-free)

__dlmconvert_master() only moves the lock between lists, so the count
entering the gap is base, list and lookup.  Drop the lookup reference
after the AST is queued instead of before it and the race ends with the
one __dlm_queue_ast() took, which dlm_flush_asts() releases later with
ast_pending cleared and ast_list unlinked.  No extra get is needed, and
the normal case ends with the same count as before.

dlmconvert_master() has the same shape but is only reached from dlmlock()
for a lock this node owns, which dlm_free_dead_locks() never matches.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/heartbeat: unlink live slots when their node is missing

o2hb_shutdown_slot() returns immediately when its node is no longer in the
configfs registry.  A slot can still be linked in o2hb_live_slots when
that lookup fails.  Region teardown or startup-error cleanup then frees
the slot array without removing its embedded list member.

With the same peer live in another region, the next list update can follow
a predecessor into the freed array.  Reusing the node number can also make
a later insertion encounter that stale member.

Always remove the slot under o2hb_live_lock, even when node lookup fails. 
Preserve aggregate membership accounting and the last-region DOWN
callback: the existing callback interface explicitly permits a NULL node
for DOWN events.  Only drop the node reference when lookup returned one. 
This closes both normal release and startup-abort paths without changing
the publication or callback locking protocol.

Also require a configured node before admitting a new live slot in
o2hb_check_slot().  The early live-bitmap check is not held through
admission: the last live slot in another region can be removed in between.
Without a node, admission can then queue an UP event with a NULL argument
and hit the event helper's BUG_ON.  Existing live slots can still leave
and generate NULL-node DOWN events.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: mce_kbd: Fix inconsistent locking of keylock

data->keylock is taken with spin_lock() in ir_mce_kbd_decode(), which
runs in the raw IR decode kthread with local interrupts enabled, but
with spin_lock_irqsave() in mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the rx_timeout timer
callback, which runs in softirq context.

If the decode kthread is holding keylock via spin_lock() when a timer
interrupt fires on the same CPU and the softirq runs
mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the softirq spins forever waiting for a lock
that only the now-preempted kthread can release, while the kthread
cannot run again until the softirq gives up the CPU. This deadlocks
the CPU.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: Ensure registered is cleared in error path

If rc_register_device() fails, ensure that registered is not set to true.
If lirc_register() succeeded, then userspace could have an open file
descriptor open. This leads to a use-after-free.

lirc_unregister() must be called with registered = false, else there is a
possibility that an fd is open and polling, which would never return
POLLERR unless registered is false.

Note that registered must be changed under dev->lock, many functions
read registered under lock (e.g. lirc_ioctl).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmet-auth: serialize access to DH-HMAC-CHAP state to fix UAF

A REPLY AUTH_SEND command can derive a dhchap_skey key while a
concurrent AUTH_RECEIVE command observing this REPLY state executes
the failure path and frees that key. The REPLY command then continues
and writes into freed memory, causing a use-after-free. KASAN reports
it as:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in __sha256_final
  Write of size 4 at addr ffff88800359c540
  ...
  nvmet_auth_sq_free (drivers/nvme/target/auth.c:237)
  nvmet_execute_auth_receive (drivers/nvme/target/fabrics-cmd-auth.c:621)

Add a mutex to each submission queue to serialize authentication
commands and timeout handling. Unlock the mutex before completing
requests and ignore outdated timeout callbacks. Limit timeout delays
to prevent immediate expiry on 32-bit kernels.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmem: core: Fix OOB read for bit offsets of more than one byte

When the bit offset is BITS_PER_BYTE or larger the read position is
advanced by `bytes_offset`. This is not taken into account in the
per-byte read loop which still reads `cell->bytes` resulting in an out of
bounds read of `bytes_offset` bytes. The information read OOB does not
leak directly as the erroneously read bits are cleared.

Detected by KASAN while looking for a use-after-free in simplefb.c.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

pps: generators: don't use the driver's info after unregister

A file that was opened before pps_gen_unregister_source() keeps
pps_gen, and with it the pointer to the driver's pps_gen_source_info.
PPS_GEN_SETENABLE and PPS_GEN_USESYSTEMCLOCK keep using that pointer
after the driver has gone:

 - pps_gen_tio allocates its info with devm_kzalloc(), so after an
   unbind both ioctls read freed memory, and SETENABLE calls the
   driver's enable() with its freed private data.

 - pps_gen-dummy does not set info->owner, so it can be unloaded while
   the file is open, and the ioctls then read the unloaded module's
   data and call its code.

TIO can't probe in a VM, as it needs ART. A test driver that registers
its info in devm memory like TIO does, unbound while /dev/pps-gen0 is
open, gives:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in pps_gen_cdev_ioctl+0x4c1/0x580
  Read of size 1 at addr ffff88800e647f38 by task ppsgen64/145
  ...
  Freed by task 146:
   kfree+0x25a/0x6d0
   release_nodes+0xd1/0x140
   devres_release_all+0x10e/0x1a0
   device_unbind_cleanup+0x71/0x250
   device_release_driver_internal+0x41b/0x570
   unbind_store+0xd9/0x100

and unloading pps_gen-dummy while its file is open oopses:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffffa0203040
  Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI
  RIP: 0010:pps_gen_cdev_ioctl+0x372/0x580

Protect info in the ioctl handler with a mutex, and clear it under the
mutex on unregister, so that unregister waits for the ioctls using it
and later ones fail with -ENODEV. PPS_KC_BIND does the same for a
removed PPS device since commit 3649f9a6b897 ("pps: don't allow
PPS_KC_BIND on removed devices"). The sysfs attributes need nothing
new: they are removed, and their callbacks drained, before info is
cleared.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

power: supply: sbs-battery: disable polling before supply teardown

The managed poll-work cancellation is registered before the power
supply, so cleanup unregisters the supply before draining polling.
A pending or running poller can then call power_supply_changed() on
the released supply.

Commit 8d59cf3887fb ("power: supply: sbs-battery: Fix use-after-free in
power_supply_changed()") moved the IRQ request after supply registration,
but did not change the poll-work cancellation order.

Add a later managed action that disables and drains polling before
supply teardown. Its retained disabled state prevents external-power
callbacks from rearming the poll work after it has been drained.
Keep the original autocancel to initialize work before supply callbacks
can run and to cover failed supply registration.

The teardown ordering issue was found by static analysis.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

power: supply: pf1550: drain IRQ work before unregistering supplies

The VBUS work calls power_supply_changed(), but its managed
cancellation is registered before the supplies. Cleanup can therefore
unregister a supply while IRQ-triggered work is still pending.

Commit 838767f50747 ("power: supply: pf1550: Fix use-after-free in
power_supply_changed()") moved IRQ requests after supply registration,
but left work cancellation before the supplies. That change protects
the direct IRQ callbacks, while this fix drains the work they queue.

Register the three work items after both supplies and before the IRQs.
Cleanup then frees the IRQ producers, drains the work, and unregisters
the supplies.

The teardown ordering issue was found by static analysis.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

phy: core: Fix race-condition between _of_phy_get() and try_module_get()

Sashiko asked during a patch review if the existing usage pattern had a
race condition; specifically in of_phy_get() if it was possible between
returning from _of_phy_get() and running try_module_get() that a module
might be unbound leading to use-after-free.

Looking at the code this appears to be so, there is no linkage between the
phy and module under a synchronisation primitive.

Using the phy_provider_mutex in phy_get() will ensure there is a link between
the returned phy pointer and the module_get() bumping the module reference
count.

Amend phy_get(), of_phy_get() and devm_of_phy_get_by_index() to fix the
same usage pattern.

phy_provider_unregister() must take the phy_provider_mutex so amending
phy_get()/of_phy_get() to take that same mutex guarantees there is no
use-after-free.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

spi: spi-pci1xxxx: quiesce DMA engines on transfer timeout

If a DMA-mapped transfer times out waiting for DMA_TERM and neither DMA
abort interrupt arrived, pci1xxxx_spi_transfer_with_dma() returns
through the error label while both DMA engines are still enabled, the
done/abort interrupt status is still armed and the transfer state
(p->xfer, p->tx_sgl, p->rx_sgl) is still registered.

The ISRs keep firing afterwards: they reprogram the DMA engines from
p->tx_sgl / p->rx_sgl and signal completion through p->xfer and
p->spi_xfer_done, all of which the SPI core is free to unmap or reuse
once transfer_one() has returned, which is a use-after-free. A late
done interrupt can also start the next transfer queued behind the
failed one.

Stop both DMA engines, drain the pending done/abort interrupt status
and synchronize the DMA IRQs before dropping the in-progress state and
the transfer pointers, and re-enable the engines afterwards so that
subsequent transfers keep working. The engines are only turned back on
once both were confirmed to have stopped: re-enabling an engine that
failed to stop would cancel the pending stop request and let it keep
running into buffers the SPI core is about to unmap or free, which is
exactly the window this patch closes. An engine that failed to stop is
left disabled, as the abort paths already do.

The DMA interrupt status and mask registers are shared between the two
SPI instances, so the cleanup drains only this instance's done/abort
status bits instead of masking the interrupt lines, which would also
suppress the peer instance's completion interrupts.

Also make the DMA ISRs ignore interrupts while no transfer is in
progress so that a stray MSI after the cleanup can no longer act on
the cleared state.

No PCI1XXXX hardware was available for testing and QEMU has no model
of this PCIe part, so the timeout path was exercised with a userspace
replica of the timeout branch and the DMA ISRs, with the register and
interrupt accesses mocked: on the unfixed code both a wedged engine
that clears after the timeout and a late done interrupt touch the
freed transfer state, while with this fix applied neither does and an
engine that failed to stop is left disabled.  The module was also
loaded and unloaded in a QEMU x86_64 guest running a kernel with this
fix applied.
